title: Important adjusting journal entries
summary: Four kinds of adjusting entry: income received in advance, outstanding expenses, prepaid expenses and income receivable, with the summary table.

chunks.heading: Unearned revenue (income received in advance)
chunks.explanation_md:
**Unearned revenue** is also called revenue received in advance, deferred revenue or income in advance. The business has the cash but has not yet earned it.

Two entries are shown:

1. When the cash arrives: **Cash/Bank A/c Dr 8500, To Interest received in advance (unearned interest) A/c 8500.** The note says cash was received from a customer for services to be performed in the future.
2. As the revenue is earned: **Interest received in advance A/c Dr 8500, To Interest A/c 8500.** This is the adjusting entry for the portion of the revenue earned.

key_terms.meaning: Revenue received in advance, also called deferred revenue or income in advance.

chunks.exam_line: Income in advance: Cash Dr to Unearned/Advance income A/c; later Unearned income A/c Dr to the income A/c for the part earned.

chunks.heading: Outstanding (accrued) expenses
chunks.explanation_md:
**Accrual of unrecorded expenses**, also called **outstanding expenses** or **payable expenses**, are costs already incurred but not yet paid.

- **Outstanding wages:** Wages Expense A/c Dr 7800, To Outstanding Wages A/c 7800. Wages earned by employees but not yet paid.
- **Outstanding interest:** Interest Expense A/c Dr, To Outstanding Interest A/c. The amount is principal × interest rate × fraction of year.
- **Outstanding income tax:** Tax Expense A/c Dr, To Outstanding Taxes A/c.

In each case the expense account is debited and a liability account is credited.

key_terms.meaning: An expense that has been incurred but not yet paid; also called accrued or payable expense.

chunks.exam_line: Outstanding expenses: Concerned Expense A/c Dr, To Outstanding Expense A/c. Interest = principal × rate × fraction of year.

chunks.heading: Prepaid expenses and income receivable
chunks.explanation_md:
**Prepaid expenses.** Rent paid in advance:

1. On payment: **Prepaid Rent A/c Dr 10,000, To Cash/Bank A/c 10,000** (cash paid in advance for rent).
2. Adjusting entry: **Rent A/c Dr 10,000, To Prepaid Rent A/c 10,000.**

**Accrued income (income receivable).** Royalty earned but not yet received:

1. **Royalty Receivable A/c Dr 5,000, To Royalty A/c 5,000** (income receivable but not yet received).
2. When the cash comes: **Cash/Bank A/c Dr, To Royalty Receivable A/c** (cash received from royalty income).
chunks.exam_line: Prepaid: Rent A/c Dr, To Prepaid Rent A/c. Income receivable: Royalty Receivable A/c Dr, To Royalty A/c.

chunks.heading: The summary table of adjusting entries
chunks.explanation_md:
The last slide puts all four types in one table:

| Adjusting entry | A/c debited | A/c credited |
|---|---|---|
| Prepaid expenses | Concerned Expense A/c | Prepaid Expense A/c |
| Unearned income / income received in advance | Unearned Revenue A/c or Income received in advance A/c | Concerned Income A/c |
| Accrued / outstanding expenses | Concerned Expense A/c | Outstanding Expense A/c or Expenses Payable A/c |
| Accrued income / income receivable | Concerned Income Receivable A/c | Concerned Revenue A/c |

Learn the table and you can write any of the adjusting entries from the earlier slides.
chunks.exam_line: Prepaid: Dr Expense, Cr Prepaid Expense. Income in advance: Dr Unearned Revenue, Cr Income. Outstanding expense: Dr Expense, Cr Outstanding Expense. Income receivable: Dr Income Receivable, Cr Revenue.

questions.stem: What is unearned revenue? Give the two journal entries shown for interest received in advance of 8500.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Unearned revenue** (also called revenue received in advance, deferred revenue or income in advance) is money received before the service is performed.

Entries:
1. On receipt: **Cash/Bank A/c Dr 8500, To Interest received in advance A/c 8500** (cash received for services to be performed in the future).
2. As earned: **Interest received in advance A/c Dr 8500, To Interest A/c 8500** (adjusting entry for the portion earned).

So the advance is first a credit to a liability-type account and later moves to income.

questions.stem: Explain outstanding expenses and give the entries for wages, interest and income tax.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Outstanding expenses** (accrual of unrecorded expenses, payable expenses) are costs incurred but not yet paid, so they must be recorded by an adjusting entry.

- **Wages:** Wages Expense A/c Dr 7800, To Outstanding Wages A/c 7800.
- **Interest:** Interest Expense A/c Dr, To Outstanding Interest A/c (principal × interest rate × fraction of year).
- **Income tax:** Tax Expense A/c Dr, To Outstanding Taxes A/c.

In each case the expense is debited and an outstanding (payable) account is credited.

questions.stem: Differentiate between prepaid expenses and outstanding expenses with the adjusting entry for each.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Prepaid expense:** paid in advance for the future. Adjusting entry: **Concerned Expense A/c Dr, To Prepaid Expense A/c**. Example: prepaid rent 10,000, Rent A/c Dr, To Prepaid Rent A/c.

**Outstanding expense:** incurred but not yet paid. Adjusting entry: **Concerned Expense A/c Dr, To Outstanding Expense A/c (or Expenses Payable A/c)**. Example: wages 7800.

In both the expense account is debited; they differ in the account credited.

rubric.point: Prepaid is paid in advance, outstanding not yet paid
Prepaid entry credits Prepaid Expense A/c
Outstanding entry credits Outstanding Expense A/c

questions.stem: Differentiate between income received in advance and accrued income (income receivable) with the debit and credit of each.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Income received in advance:** cash is received before the income is earned. As it is earned: **Unearned Revenue A/c (or Income received in advance A/c) Dr, To Concerned Income A/c**.

**Accrued income:** income is earned but not yet received. **Concerned Income Receivable A/c Dr, To Concerned Revenue A/c**. Example: Royalty Receivable A/c Dr 5,000, To Royalty A/c 5,000.

One starts with cash and later earns it; the other starts with earning and later receives cash.

questions.stem: Explain the four types of adjusting journal entry with the debit and credit for each and an example from the slides.
questions.model_answer_md:
Adjusting entries bring the books in line with what has actually been earned or incurred in the period. Four types are shown.

1. **Prepaid expenses:** Dr Concerned Expense A/c, Cr Prepaid Expense A/c. Example: Prepaid Rent A/c Dr 10,000, To Cash/Bank A/c on payment, then Rent A/c Dr 10,000, To Prepaid Rent A/c.
2. **Unearned income (income received in advance):** Dr Unearned Revenue A/c or Income received in advance A/c, Cr Concerned Income A/c. Example: cash of 8500 received in advance, then Interest received in advance A/c Dr 8500, To Interest A/c 8500.
3. **Accrued or outstanding expenses:** Dr Concerned Expense A/c, Cr Outstanding Expense A/c or Expenses Payable A/c. Example: Wages Expense A/c Dr 7800, To Outstanding Wages A/c 7800; also outstanding interest (principal × interest rate × fraction of year) and outstanding tax.
4. **Accrued income (income receivable):** Dr Concerned Income Receivable A/c, Cr Concerned Revenue A/c. Example: Royalty Receivable A/c Dr 5,000, To Royalty A/c 5,000, and later Cash/Bank A/c Dr, To Royalty Receivable A/c.

In every case one side is the concerned income or expense account, so the profit of the period is stated correctly.

questions.stem: Show, with journal entries, how prepaid rent of 10,000 and royalty receivable of 5,000 are handled from the first entry to the final one.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Prepaid rent of 10,000**

1. When paid: **Prepaid Rent A/c Dr 10,000, To Cash/Bank A/c 10,000** (cash paid in advance for rent).
2. Adjusting entry: **Rent A/c Dr 10,000, To Prepaid Rent A/c 10,000**.

By the summary table, a prepaid expense debits the concerned expense account and credits the prepaid expense account.

**Royalty receivable of 5,000**

1. Adjusting entry: **Royalty Receivable A/c Dr 5,000, To Royalty A/c 5,000** (income receivable but not yet received).
2. When the cash comes in: **Cash/Bank A/c Dr, To Royalty Receivable A/c** (cash received from royalty income).

By the summary table, accrued income debits the concerned income receivable account and credits the concerned revenue account.
